description: Content Service operational dashboard — saturation, latency breakdown, failure modes. Drives load-test reads.

panels.description:
- Concurrent in-flight Fetch calls, per pod.
- GLOBAL_MAX_INFLIGHT (default 200) is a per-pod cap — compare the red line to the per-pod lines, not the total-across-pods line.
- Plateaued at the cap → requests are queueing in the semaphore; queue time shows up as request latency.
panels.title: In-flight requests (global vs stream)

panels.description:
- Request rate by status. Sustained `failed` is the load-test failure signal.
- Counted per DELIVERY, not per document — a Nak'd + redelivered message counts as a failure AND (if the retry succeeds) a completion.
- A burst of redeliveries raises every status line at once, including `completed` — don't read that as broad recovery.
- For NATS-only failure reasons, see "NATS retry outcomes" below.
panels.title: Request rate by status

panels.description: - End-to-end Fetch latency p50/p95/p99, across all api + content_type combinations.
panels.title: Request latency (p50/p95/p99)

panels.description:
- Rejections by reason. Non-zero → hit a concurrency ceiling.
- reason ∈ {global_full, stream_full, shutdown}.
panels.title: Rejections by reason

panels.description:
- Cache S3 op latency p99, by bucket/op — isolates S3 latency from content-service code paths.
- Since 2026-08, hits are served HEAD-only (bodies delivered via CacheLocation) — `get` volume should be a small fraction of `head`.
- Rising `get` rate → the extraction path or the sha256 safety-net is doing real reads.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, bucket, op) (rate(content_cache_op_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[1m])))

panels.title: Cache op p99 latency (by bucket/op)

panels.description:
- NATS fetch outcomes/sec by connector. outcome ∈ {completed, pickup_timeout, worker_timeout, canceled, error}.
- Non-zero `pickup_timeout` → connectors aren't keeping up.
- Non-zero `worker_timeout` → connectors are stuck mid-fetch.
panels.title: NATS fetch outcomes by connector

panels.description:
- Three independent ratios — they answer different questions and don't move together.
- "Direct RAW request — served from cache": plain RAW-request hits (phase=fetch). Drop → RAW callers increasingly missing.
- "TEXT request — raw already cached": the raw-bucket check before extraction (phase=extract). Low/red → TEXT requests are paying for a connector round-trip before extraction even starts.
- "TEXT request — text already cached": final extracted output already cached — the cheapest possible outcome.
- No data on a tile = zero traffic on that path, not a ratio of zero.
- Red tile on unique-document traffic (first-pass scan) is expected. Red tile on repeat-document traffic is worth investigating.

targets.expr: sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="raw", phase="fetch"}[5m])) / (sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="raw", phase="fetch"}[5m])) + sum(rate(content_cache_misses_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="raw", phase="fetch"}[5m])))
targets.legendFormat: Direct RAW request — served from cache

sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="text", phase="extract"}[5m])) / (sum(rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="text", phase="extract"}[5m])) + sum(rate(content_cache_misses_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", bucket="text", phase="extract"}[5m])))

panels.description:

- Only `success`/`failed` populate the histogram — `skipped`/`breaker_open` record duration=0 by design.

panels.description:
- NATS two-phase reply latency p99 by connector. pickup = publish→PROCESSING; worker = PROCESSING→COMPLETED.
- Both timeouts default to 30s — p99 climbing toward 30s means timeouts are imminent.
- Pair with "NATS fetch outcomes" for the actual timeout counts.

- Covers stream ingest + S3 upload; excludes the sha256 stamp copy (own panel).
- Buckets explicit since 2026-08 — earlier data read 10–1000x too high (SDK's ms-scale default buckets).

panels.description:
- Placeholder — content-service emits no `content_extraction_circuit_state` today; shows No data by design.
- Will start working unchanged once the extractor circuit breaker (xberg backpressure work) ships (0=closed / 1=half-open / 2=open).
- Until then, use "Retry attempts by error code": a rising SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE line is what a breaker would trip on.

panels.description: - S3 cache operation errors/sec. error_type ∈ {read_failed, write_failed, other}.

panels.title: Cache op errors (by error_type)

panels.description:
- Cache write outcomes from S3Store. result ∈ {success, read_error, size_mismatch, s3_error, canceled, timeout}.
- `timeout` → CACHE_WRITE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS fired.
- `size_mismatch` also deletes the truncated object.
panels.title: Cache write outcomes

panels.description: - Requests FAILED during graceful shutdown drain. Should be ~0 except during deploy/restart.
panels.title: Shutdown-time failures

panels.description:
- Fires when a raw object has no sha256 metadata (normally stamped synchronously at write time) — should be ~0 outside legacy objects aging out of the 7d raw TTL.
- Steady `computed_in_process` → stamping regression.
- `raw_head_miss_text_hit` → text served after its raw was evicted, and the text object predates the sha stamp.
panels.title: sha256 safety-net activations

panels.description:
- Text extraction outcomes/sec. status ∈ {success, failed, skipped, breaker_open}.
- `skipped` tracking near `success` → large share of TEXT requests exceed EXTRACTION_MAX_SIZE (deployed 50 MiB) and are served raw with no extraction — confirm this matches the expected corpus mix.
- Sustained `breaker_open` → kreuzberg is unhealthy and content-service stopped sending it work; expect SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE to climb on "Retry attempts by error code" too.
- Rising `failed` with flat `success` → documents failing extraction outright (corrupt/unsupported), not a capacity problem.
- `success` alone doesn't show cost — pair with "Extraction p99 latency".
panels.title: Extraction outcomes

panels.description:
- Distribution of bytes written per S3 cache Put — p50/p95/p99.
- Bodies over the 16 MiB multipart threshold take the multipart upload path.
- 5m window (wider than other panels) — write events are infrequent and benefit from smoothing.
- Buckets explicit (4KiB–5GiB) since 2026-08; earlier data used ms-scale defaults and is unreadable.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_write_bytes_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_write_bytes_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_write_bytes_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m])))

panels.title: Cache write size distribution

panels.description:
- Splits successful raw-write latency: `total p95` = whole write (connector stream read + S3 PutObject); `stream-wait p95` = time blocked reading the connector.
- total − stream-wait ≈ S3-side time.
- `stream-wait` ≈ `total` → the connector/source system is slow, not the cache.
- `stream-wait` small, `total` high → S3 itself is slow.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(content_cache_write_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", result="success"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(content_cache_write_stream_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", result="success"}[5m])))

panels.title: Raw cache write p95 — time waiting on connector vs. total

panels.description:
- How long abandoned writes ran before dying. `canceled` = peer went away (connector crash, pod eviction, client deadline). `timeout` = CACHE_WRITE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS fired.
- Kept separate from the main latency panel — this is client-abandonment behavior, not cache performance.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_write_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", result=~"canceled|timeout"}[5m])))

panels.title: Cache write — abandoned transfers (canceled/timeout)

panels.description:
- Post-upload sha256 stamp (server-side CopyObject self-copy), synchronous within Put but excluded from write-duration.
- Cost scales with object size — up to the 5GB CopyObject ceiling.
- Sustained `error` → objects left unstamped → sha safety-net activations rise downstream.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_sha_stamp_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m])))

panels.title: sha256 stamp (CopyObject) p95 by result

panels.description:
- Writes where the connector declared no size, so byte-count validation was skipped.
- Should be ~0 — sustained rate means a connector is uploading unverifiable (possibly truncated) content.
panels.title: Unverified writes (no declared size)

panels.description:
- Upload streams currently admitted. Each holds ~48–64MiB of transfer-manager buffers.
- Capped service-wide at UPLOAD_MAX_CONCURRENT (default 32, red line).
- Sustained saturation → connectors are queueing behind the gate.
panels.title: Upload streams in flight (cap 32)
Retry amplification — how one connector error becomes a platform stall (NXE-2480)

panels.description:
- Connector fetches per document actually drained by the privacy pipeline. 1.0 = healthy (fetched exactly once).
- Retry ladder ceiling = extractRetryMaxAttempts (5) × JetStream MaxDeliver (3) = 15 — approaching 15 means failing documents consume the whole ladder while holding a caller's worker.
- Reads true only while a privacy scan is running (pii_* is emitted by the privacy job).
panels.title: Fetch amplification (fetches per document)

panels.description:
- `failed_budget` — read this one first, it's the common outcome. CALLER_WAIT_BUDGET_SECONDS (5s) stopped the retry ladder early, replied to the caller, then Nak'd with a 30s delay.
- `failed` — in-handler attempts exhausted, or a malformed request / non-retryable manager failure. Rising `failed` means documents are being retried, not that callers are stranded.
- `failed_terminal` — MaxDeliver reached or budget spent on the last delivery. Replies AND Acks — end of the line for that document.
- `failed_draining` — a pod refusing new extraction work while shutting down; Nak'd for a healthy replica to pick up.
- All four should sit near 0 in steady state; all four ran sustained through the 2026-07-27 incident.
- Shows THAT and WHY (of these 4 reasons) a delivery was Nak'd, not the underlying connector/extraction error — for that, check "Retry attempts by error code" or the Warn log at the Nak decision point.
panels.title: NATS retry outcomes — failed vs budget vs terminal vs draining (per delivery)

panels.description:
- Should sit at ~0.
- Rising → requests exceed the histogram's 60s top bucket; every p95/p99 on this dashboard understates the real tail — go to "Request latency" / "Extraction p99 latency" to find the slow phase.
- A steady, near-constant (not spiky) value is the 2026-07-27 outage pattern: p95 pinned at 29s because 100% of requests sat in the same interpolated bucket.
- Ceiling is 60s because the service allows pickup 60s + worker 180s = 240s end-to-end, but the histogram's top bucket stops at 60s.
- Query gotcha: the bucket label is decimal (`le="60.0"`) — `le="60"` silently matches nothing.

targets.expr: sum(rate(content_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", api="nats", le="+Inf"}[5m])) - sum(rate(content_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", api="nats", le="60.0"}[5m]))

panels.title: Requests past the 60s top bucket

panels.description:
- Privacy document throughput vs. the rate below which its OpenSearch Point-in-Time lease expires.
- Critical rate = 32 consumers × 1000-doc pages ÷ 30-min lease = 17.8 docs/s (red line).
- Sustained operation below the red line → PIT lease expires → 404 search_context_missing_exception, and the scan then reports SUCCESS having read only part of the index (reader error is discarded).
- Requires a running privacy scan.
panels.title: Privacy throughput vs the PIT critical rate

panels.description:
- Time spent waiting for an extraction slot before reaching xberg — separates "we queued" from "xberg was slow", which otherwise surface as the same error codes.
- Rising p95 + "Extraction slots in use" pinned at capacity → a queueing problem, not a document problem.
- Split by lane: `interactive` wait climbing toward `bulk` → the priority lane (EXTRACTION_PRIORITY_MAX_CONSECUTIVE) isn't buying anything anymore.
- Buckets run to 600s — the extraction semaphore has no acquire timeout.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, lane) (rate(content_extraction_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="admitted"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, lane) (rate(content_extraction_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="admitted"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, lane) (rate(content_extraction_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="admitted"}[5m])))

panels.title: Extraction queue wait (admitted)

panels.description:
- Slot occupancy (count, 0–60, left axis) vs. `aborted/s` (rate, right axis) — different units, check the legend value, not just line height.
- Occupancy capped at EXTRACTION_MAX_CONCURRENCY — deployed value 60 (code default 10; confirm `contentService.env` before trusting the red line).
- Occupancy saturates: once pinned it can't show how far behind you are — use "Extraction queue wait" for that.
- Sustained `aborted/s` > 0 → the gate is shedding work (deadline expired while queueing), not just pacing it.
- Per-lane split shows who holds the gate: `bulk` filling it during a scan is expected, interactive extractions should still get in. No line for a lane = no traffic, not zero.
panels.title: Extraction concurrency (cap 60) — occupied slots (count) vs. abandoned-wait rate (req/s)

panels.description:
- A rising line = a specific error is driving repeated in-handler retries.
- `EXTRACTION_ERROR_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` rising → kreuzberg is refusing work (overloaded) — retrying it makes the backlog worse, not better.
- `EXTRACTION_ERROR_TIMEOUT` → documents genuinely slow to extract (capped at fewer attempts — a timeout will likely repeat).
- `CONTENT_ERROR_CACHE_WRITE_FAILED` → check S3/cache health, not the extractor.
- `CONTENT_ERROR_INTERNAL` → the connector's source system (Box/SharePoint/etc.) is unreachable or rate-limiting it — a source-side problem.
panels.title: Retry attempts by error code

panels.description:
- One line per (code, retryable) — use `code` to trace an error spike back to specific URNs.
- `retryable=true` → content-service retries automatically. `retryable=false` rising → documents need a human or a source-side fix.
- `CACHE_WRITE_FAILED` is always retryable (our own S3 write treated as transient).
- `TOO_LARGE` is essentially never retryable — the source object exceeds the connector's size limit.
- `CONNECTOR_UNAVAILABLE` = no connector answered within PICKUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS — the request isn't lost, it stays queued on CONTENT_FETCH.
panels.title: Connector fetch errors by code

panels.description:
- Valkey claims taken before a connector fetch or an xberg extraction, so two replicas don't duplicate work. Expect everything but `won` at 0 until KEDA scales past one replica.
- `won` → this pod took the claim and is doing the work.
- `lost` → another replica holds it; this pod waits for the output instead.
- `preempted` → interactive work took a bulk holder's claim — a deliberate duplicate (the displaced holder keeps working).
- `held_by_self` → this pod found its own earlier claim (usually a fetch claim outliving a reply timeout) — a connector slowdown, not a dedup event.
- `duplicated` → gave up waiting and did the work anyway (interactive requests only — no redelivery to defer to).
- `lease_lost` → a renewal found the claim gone mid-work — leading indicator of duplicate work.
- `unavailable` → Valkey unreachable, dedup silently degraded (still correct, just costs duplicate fetches/extractions).
- `disabled` → dedup off for that phase (VALKEY_HOST unset, or that phase's TTL zeroed) — should be flat 0 when configured correctly.
- Watch `disabled` (likely misconfiguration) and `lease_lost` (duplicate work happening now) most closely.
panels.title: Cross-pod dedup — claim outcomes

panels.description:
- Rising `peer`/`satisfied` → dedup paying off (waited instead of repeating a fetch/extraction).
- Rising `connector` → NOT dedup — this request's own claim's connector reply timed out; read as connector slowness.
- Rising `took_over` → escalate. The previous claim holder died mid-work and this request redid it. Steady trickle = normal pod recycling; a spike = replicas dying under load.
- `peer` scales with replica count/hot keys; `connector` scales with source-system load — not substitutes for each other.
- `extract` is always `peer`, never `connector` — extraction is synchronous, nothing can outlive it the way a fetch can.
- Any non-`satisfied` outcome = a missed optimization, never a failure.
- `skipped` = no deadline left to wait within (PEER_WAIT_SECONDS / CONNECTOR_WAIT_SECONDS / GET_CONTENT_DEADLINE_SECONDS) — high `skipped` next to flat `satisfied` is a timing-budget problem; retune those seconds, don't chase the claim logic.
- `expired` (someone still working) and `took_over` (nobody was working) look identical in wall-clock terms but mean opposite things.

targets.expr: sum by (phase, source, outcome) (rate(content_dedup_waits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod"}[5m]))

panels.title: Cross-pod dedup — work avoided vs redone

panels.description:
- How long a wait took before it paid off, split by who was waited on. Filtered to outcome="satisfied" — an expired wait always equals its full budget and would flatten every quantile onto the ceiling.
- PEER_WAIT_SECONDS bounds a peer wait, CONNECTOR_WAIT_SECONDS a connector wait, GET_CONTENT_DEADLINE_SECONDS caps both (same number in dev today only because PEER_WAIT_SECONDS isn't templated).
- `fetch/peer` ≈ connector latency + remaining holder lease. `fetch/connector` = how far past our own reply timeout the connector ran — use to size PICKUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS / the worker timeout. `extract/peer` = how long another replica's xberg run took.
- p50/p95 only. Buckets run to 600s — waits should stay well under that.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, phase, source) (rate(content_dedup_wait_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="satisfied"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, phase, source) (rate(content_dedup_wait_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", pod=~"$pod", outcome="satisfied"}[5m])))

panels.title: Cross-pod dedup — how long a paying wait took

panels.description:
- Extractions that finished after the caller left — deliberate, not a leak: canceling xberg mid-flight throws the whole run away, since nothing persists until it returns. Letting it finish means the caller's retry finds cached text instead of re-running.
- Cost: an extraction slot held for a caller who's gone — pair with "Extraction slots in use": rising count while the gate is pinned means part of capacity is committed to callers who left.
- Steady low rate = design working as intended (bulk requests hitting their delivery deadline).
- Sustained `interactive` is worse than `bulk` — a human gave up waiting; check GET_CONTENT_DEADLINE_SECONDS against the extraction phase before tuning anything else.
panels.title: Extractions that outlived their caller
KEDA inflight trigger — baseline before retuning the threshold
What the autoscaler sees vs what is really in flight
panels.description:
- The KEDA trigger runs sum(content_inflight_global) with NO label filter — the series to check before changing the inflight threshold (default 100) or activationThreshold (default 20).
- Inflated by (1) dual scrape — every pod is scraped twice (kubernetes-services + PodMonitor), doubling an unfiltered sum(); the NATS triggers use max() so they're unaffected, this is the only sum()-based trigger — and (2) no namespace filter — a shared Prometheus counts every namespace, not just $namespace.
- Divide by threshold to get the replicas this trigger is asking for. KEDA takes the highest count any trigger requests.

targets.legendFormat: stream gauge — zero means a pre-fix build

panels.title: Replicas this trigger is asking for
panels.description:
- ceil(KEDA query / threshold), clamped to maxReplicas (default 5).
- Red at 5 → pinned at the ceiling — can no longer tell "full" from "far behind"; avoid this state when picking a new threshold.
- Admission gate caps globalMaxInflight (deployed 200) per pod — a hard ceiling on the gauge itself.

panels.title: Request rate: See Content (gRPC) vs NATS (bulk)
panels.description:
- content_inflight_global has no scope label — request rate by api is the closest proxy: grpc_get_content / grpc_fetch_stream = See Content, nats = scan lane.
- As of 2026-08-19 no production caller uses gRPC — both See Content series should read flat zero.
- If flat zero, the KEDA threshold doesn't need to move — nothing new is being added to the sum since the IncInflight scope fix.

- Where a request's bytes actually came from, by request type.
- Rising "text already cached" → TEXT requests answered with zero backend work.
- Rising "raw already cached" + flat "raw not cached" → TEXT misses are cheap (extraction only, no connector round-trip).
- Rising "raw not cached" → TEXT requests paying for a connector fetch AND an extraction — the most expensive path.
- "Direct RAW request" lines answer the same question for plain RAW requests, which never run extraction.
- Caveat: a text-cache miss is counted once per request, but the raw-bucket check underneath is deduplicated across concurrent requests for the same URN (singleflight) — counts aren't guaranteed to add up 1:1 during a concurrent burst.

targets.legendFormat: TEXT request — text already cached (no work needed)
TEXT request — raw already cached (extracted fresh, no connector call)
TEXT request — raw not cached (connector fetch required)
Direct RAW request — served from cache
Direct RAW request — fetched from connector

panels.title: Cache path outcome — TEXT (extract) vs RAW (fetch)

panels.description:
- Raw read = rate(content_cache_read_bytes_sum{bucket="raw"}) — bytes returned by cache Gets (sha256 safety-net + pre-extraction raw reads).
- Raw write = rate(content_cache_write_bytes_sum) — bytes PUT into the raw bucket by S3Store (connector uploads).
- Text write = rate(content_text_cache_stored_bytes_total) — compressed text bytes PUT into the text bucket.
- No "text read" line — content-service never reads the text body back out. Text hits are served HEAD-only (CacheLocation-only delivery); the caller fetches bytes directly from S3, invisible to this service.
- Raw read ≫ raw write, sustained → repeat reads of already-cached raw objects (sha256 safety-net or pre-extraction lookups on a hot document).
- Text write ≪ raw write → most raw traffic is RAW requests or direct-store bypasses, not going through extraction.
panels.title: Cache bytes/sec — read vs write, raw vs text

panels.description:
- Sent = rate(content_extraction_bytes_sent_total) by parser_kind — content bytes handed to kreuzberg/tika, recorded regardless of outcome.
- Received = rate(content_extraction_bytes_received_total) by parser_kind — extracted text bytes returned, success only.
- Received ≪ sent → extraction is compressing, as expected for text-dense documents (PDFs/Office docs shrink a lot). A ratio near 1 on a compressible corpus is worth a second look.
- `tika` series only appear when EXTRACTION_COMPARISON_ENABLED=true (shadow-run comparison) — flat/missing tika lines in normal operation are expected, not a gap.
- Sent rising with no matching rise in received → extraction attempts are failing — check "Extraction outcomes".
panels.title: Extraction bytes/sec — sent vs received, by parser
